claims.text: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has poor oxygen resistance.
Adding about 1–2 at.% Al to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote formation of an Al2O3 surface scale during high-temperature exposure to air.
The Al2O3 surface scale will be protective.
Al in the alloy will locally oxidize to produce a dense Al2O3 scale.
The dense Al2O3 scale will act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
Restricting oxygen ingress with the Al2O3 scale will prevent oxygen-induced embrittlement.
The proposed Al addition will improve oxidation resistance in air at 1000 °C for exposures up to 100 hours.
The Al-modified alloy will retain a yield strength of at least 163 MPa at 1000 °C.
The Al-modified alloy will maintain ductility relative to unmodified cast HfNbTaTiZr.
The predicted oxidation and mechanical-performance benefits apply under uniaxial loading at strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
Oxygen infiltration during oxidizing high-temperature exposure compromises the ductility of untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen infiltration during oxidizing high-temperature exposure compromises the strength of untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr.
Al contents above approximately 3 at.% may cause undesirable phase formation.
Al contents above approximately 3 at.% may decrease mechanical properties.

contradictions.description: The design simultaneously specifies a constant tensile load and a prescribed strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1. Constant-load and strain-rate-controlled tests are distinct loading modes unless the strain rate is merely measured rather than imposed.

The hypothesis promises no reduction in strength, but the stated threshold of at least 163 MPa does not ensure strength retention relative to an untreated baseline that is stated to reach as high as 530 MPa.

The predicted outcome requires comparable strength and maintained ductility, whereas the falsification rule requires superior strength and ductility; the latter is a stricter and different mechanical criterion.
